text:
There isn't one best combo, because it depends on whether you run the roof AC. The right pick turns on three things: your biggest startup load, your daily watt-hours, and the unit's solar input limit. A 13,500 BTU roof AC draws about 1,500W running and spikes past 3,000W at startup, so a small unit won't start it ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).

**Weekends, no AC (fridge, Starlink, laptop, CPAP)**
- **EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus** (1,024Wh, 1,800W, up to 1,000W solar input, about 28 lb, expandable to 5kWh) was ranked best overall for camping. Pair it with two 500W-capable panel inputs for the fastest solar refill, though a single 200W panel also works, just slower ([Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)).
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2** (1,070Wh, 1,500W, about 23.8 lb) is the simplest and lightest. Its solar input caps at 400W, so two 200W SolarSaga panels is the most it can use, and it isn't expandable ([same review](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)).

**Multi-day boondocking, mid-size**
- **BLUETTI AC200L** (2,048Wh, 2,400W, up to 1,200W solar, built-in 30A RV outlet, about 62 lb) is the value pick ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/), [Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)). It can't start a roof AC on its own, since its surge rating is 3,600W with 2,400W continuous.

**Running the roof AC or full-timing**
- **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3** (4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous, 8,000W surge, expandable past 12kWh) was the top RV pick. One battery runs a 13,500 BTU AC for roughly 2.3 hours, or about two days of fridge, lights, laptop and Starlink. It's heavy enough to need two people to lift ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).
- **Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro** (3,024Wh, 3,000W, 6,000W surge) can start an AC without a soft-start kit, per the same review.
- **ALLPOWERS R4000** (3,456Wh, 3,600W at 120V, 6,000W peak, RV outlet, up to 2,000W solar over three inputs, 5-year warranty, 45 kg) is the one I have a direct buy link for. It lists at $1,499 and code ALLPOWERS26 (10% off sitewide, through 12/30) brings it to about $1,349. [Buy at ALLPOWERS](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh) (affiliate link, no extra cost to you). Each of the three solar inputs tops out at 650W, so you need panels on all three to reach 2,000W ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/allpowers-r4000-3456wh)). It's also heavy.

**Solar panel sizing**
- Match your panels to the station's solar input limit. Extra panel wattage beyond that is wasted, as with the Jackery's 400W cap.
- For rooftop arrays, check the voltage range as well as the wattage.
- One source suggests 300W to 400W of folding panels will refill a mid-size unit in a full day of decent sun ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).
- A Renogy 200W solar suitcase was suggested as a pairing for 1,000Wh units ([NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife)).

**Caveats**
- My search results didn't include direct purchase links for the EcoFlow, Jackery or BLUETTI models, only review pages, so check current prices on the manufacturer or Amazon listings.
- Many of these pages are affiliate sites.
- If you plug into the RV's shore inlet, use a proper adapter (a TT-30 dogbone for 30A). Have an electrician do any hardwired connection.

If you tell me whether you run the AC, how many nights off-grid, and your budget, I can narrow this to one unit and a matching panel setup.
